Blockchain randomness must be not only random, but verifiable. Otherwise “random” becomes trust in whoever pressed the button.

➡️ South Korea confirms 22% crypto tax will cover private wallets, foreign exchanges 

🌐 South Korea has confirmed that taxable crypto income earned through overseas exchanges and private wallets will fall under its planned 22% digital asset tax when the regime takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027. Digital Asset reported on Aug. 20, citing government responses submitted to People Power Party lawmaker Kim Sang-hoon, that the Ministry of Economy and Finance and the National Tax Service said the location or custody method of a digital asset would not determine whether income from its transfer or lending is taxable. 

⭐️ Under the current framework, income from digital assets will be classified as other income, with an annual basic deduction of 2.5 million won. Income exceeding that threshold will face a 20% national tax, rising to a maximum combined rate of 22% after local income tax. The government also maintained that the tax should take effect on schedule next year, even as the People Power Party continues to call for its abolition or another delay.

⚡️ The National Tax Service said income earned by South Korean residents through the transfer or lending of digital assets would remain taxable regardless of whether the assets were held on an overseas exchange or in a private wallet. The Finance Ministry gave a similar response, saying the tax treatment does not depend on whether the income originated domestically or overseas. Transactions made through private wallets will also be treated under the same principle.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz addressed Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Turkish this week. He accused the Turkish president of dragging Turkey into “dangerous adventures in Syria” and warned that Israel would not allow anyone to threaten its security.

Katz told Erdogan to confine himself to the speeches he gives in Turkey’s parliament — speeches that are, in Katz’s words, “detached from reality” — rather than test Israel’s resolve. 

Turkey’s Defense Ministry replied with a denial and a promise.

No Turkish military delegation was at Abu al-Duhur air base before or during Israel’s strike, Ankara said. Turkey also said Israeli operations against neighboring countries must not be normalized. It pledged to keep helping Syria build its own military capacity and infrastructure under the “one army” principle. 

No Turkish presence at the base. Continued Turkish help to build the military that will use it.

Syria’s foreign minister, Asaad al-Shaibani, also denied that Ankara was building a base at Abu al-Duhur. He told Axios there was no plan for a permanent Turkish deployment or Turkish forces at the airfield. The base, he said, was largely empty and was being restored for the Syrian Air Force. Turkish officers had visited for training and broader military cooperation. 

Shaibani also confirmed that Israel and Syria had discussed Turkish military activity in Syria before the strike. Reuters reported that he and Mossad chief Roman Gofman spoke by phone on August 14, with Turkish deployments, arms transfers, drones, and military assistance to Syria among the issues discussed. 

Israel says it warned Damascus not to permit a Turkish deployment at the base. Damascus says no such deployment was planned. Both accounts agree that Turkey’s military role in Syria was important enough to discuss before Israel bombed the runway.

Shaibani said Israel had no legitimate justification for the attack. He added that U.S.-mediated talks on a security arrangement had made significant progress, but that Israel later walked back its commitments and the agreement was never implemented. 

The official denials were followed by a less restrained message from inside Syria’s ruling family.

Hussein al-Sharaa, father of President Ahmed al-Sharaa, wrote on Facebook that Damascus’s restraint reflected international considerations and reconstruction needs, not weakness. Syrians, he said, could raise large fighting forces within days. “We have occupied land called the Golan Heights,” he wrote. “We will take it back — sooner or later.” 

Hezbollah’s parliamentary bloc in Lebanon, which Damascus has worked to weaken, also condemned the Israeli strike as a violation of Syrian sovereignty. The statement put Hezbollah on the same side as a Syrian government working to cut Hezbollah’s own supply lines. 

Israel says it is preventing a Turkish threat. Turkey says it is supporting a Syrian army. Damascus says there was no Turkish deployment to prevent.
